summary: The council hands Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor, who questions Him privately about His kingship, finds no fault in Him, and marvels at His silence.
key_insight: All four Gospels give Pilate’s first question to Jesus in exactly the same words: “Are You the King of the Jews?” Jesus does not deny it. He tells Pilate what kind of King He is: His kingdom is not of this world, and He came to bear witness to the truth.
story: They bound Jesus and led Him away to Pontius Pilate the governor. {Mt} It was early morning. They brought Him to the Praetorium, but they did not go in themselves, lest they should be defiled, so that they might eat the Passover. {Jn}

So Pilate went out to them. “What accusation do you bring against this Man?” They answered, “If He were not an evildoer, we would not have delivered Him up to you.” Pilate said, “You take Him and judge Him according to your law.” They replied, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” This fulfilled what Jesus had said about the kind of death He would die. {Jn} Then they began to accuse Him: “We found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to pay taxes to Caesar, saying that He Himself is Christ, a King.” {Lk}

Pilate went back into the Praetorium, called Jesus, and asked Him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” Jesus answered, “Are you speaking for yourself about this, or did others tell you this concerning Me?” “Am I a Jew?” said Pilate. “Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered You to me. What have You done?” {Jn}

Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If My kingdom were of this world, My servants would fight, so that I should not be delivered to the Jews; but now My kingdom is not from here.” “Are You a king then?” Pilate asked. Jesus answered, “You say rightly that I am a king. For this cause I was born, and for this cause I have come into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears My voice.” Pilate said to Him, “What is truth?” {Jn}

Then Pilate went out again and told the chief priests and the crowd, “I find no fault in this Man.” {Lk} The chief priests accused Him of many things, but He answered nothing. Pilate asked Him again, “Do You answer nothing? See how many things they testify against You!” {Mk} But He answered him not one word, so that the governor marveled greatly. {Mt}
The accusers grew more fierce: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee to this place.” {Lk}
differences: Only John records the leaders staying outside, their statement that they could not put anyone to death, and the private conversation inside the Praetorium.
Only Luke lists the charges and Pilate’s first verdict, “I find no fault in this Man,” and the accusers’ mention of Galilee.
In Matthew, Mark and Luke Jesus answers Pilate, “It is as you say.” In John He first answers with a question and then speaks of His kingdom.
Matthew and Mark record Jesus’ silence before His accusers and Pilate’s amazement.

fit.question: Matthew, Mark and Luke give Jesus a brief answer, “It is as you say,” and then silence. John records a long conversation. Did Jesus speak to Pilate or not?

points.label: Inside and outside
points.text: John says Pilate called Jesus into the Praetorium and talked with Him there, away from the accusers, who would not enter. Outside, facing the chief priests’ charges, Jesus answered nothing (Matthew, Mark). He answered the judge’s question about His kingship, but He made no reply to the charges, even when Pilate pressed Him.

points.label: Short form and long form
points.text: “It is as you say” is the short form of what John gives in full: “You say rightly that I am a king.” The other Gospels report the answer; John reports the conversation around it.

fit.note: John fills in the private part of the hearing that the other Gospels summarize. Their accounts fit together naturally.
fit.short: Jesus spoke with Pilate privately inside (John) and was silent before His accusers outside (Matthew, Mark). “It is as you say” summarizes His answer.

scene.label: Pontius Pilate
scene.text: Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 bears his name and that title. He normally lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem with troops at the feasts. Philo and Josephus describe him as harsh and stubborn.

scene.label: The Praetorium
scene.text: This was the governor’s headquarters in Jerusalem, probably Herod the Great’s former palace on the city’s western hill. Some place it at the Antonia Fortress beside the temple.

scene.label: Defilement
scene.text: Many Jews held that entering a Gentile’s house made a person ceremonially unclean (compare Acts 10:28). So the leaders stood outside. They guarded their cleanness for the feast while pressing for an innocent man’s death. (On how “eat the Passover” fits the Passover meal of the night before, see event 141.)

scene.label: No power of death
scene.text: Under Roman rule the right to execute belonged to the governor. Josephus reports that when a later high priest, Ananus, a son of Annas, had James, the brother of Jesus, stoned in AD 62 while no governor was in the province, he was removed from office for it.

scene.label: Taxes to Caesar
scene.text: The charge was false. When asked about paying taxes in the temple only days before, Jesus had said, “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke 20:25).

witnesses.matthew: Calls Pilate “the governor” again and again and stresses Jesus’ silence: “not one word,” so that the governor “marveled greatly.” The King stands before Rome’s governor and does not defend Himself.
witnesses.mark: Is very brief: one question, one answer, then silence and Pilate’s amazement. The Jesus who spoke with authority throughout Mark’s Gospel now says almost nothing.
witnesses.luke: Lists the political charges, each framed to alarm a Roman, and gives Pilate’s first verdict: “I find no fault in this Man.” Luke records Pilate declaring Jesus innocent three times (23:4, 14, 22), part of his careful case that Jesus was no rebel against Rome.
witnesses.john: Takes us inside the Praetorium for the conversation about kingdom and truth. John notes the leaders’ concern for purity and that a Roman death fulfilled Jesus’ own words “signifying by what death He would die” (John 12:32–33): He would be lifted up from the earth.

seeing.reveals: Jesus stands before Rome’s governor as a King whose kingdom does not come from this world and who was born to bear witness to the truth. Pilate asks, “What is truth?” while the One who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life,” stands in front of him (John 14:6).
seeing.living: Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by servants who fight; it gathers people who are “of the truth” and hear His voice. Listen for His voice above the noise of accusation and politics, and do not try to defend His kingdom with the weapons of this world.
seeing.ponder: Pilate asked, “What is truth?” and walked out without waiting for an answer. Are you staying long enough to hear Jesus’ voice?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus is a King whose kingdom is not from here, and His people hear His voice.
outline: A kingdom not of this world (36)
A King who bears witness to the truth (37–38)
preaching.watch_for: Watch Pilate move: out to the leaders (v. 29), in to Jesus (v. 33), out again (v. 38), and so on through 19:16. John’s trial swings between the crowd outside and Jesus inside, and Pilate is caught between them.
